# 1. Introduction

The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in K–12 education is increasingly recognized for its potential benefits (Annamalai, [2025; ](#funding)Chiu, 2024; Crompton et al., 2024; Du et al. 2024; Martin et al., 2023; Velander et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025). As a pedagogical tool and aid (Edwards & Cheok, 2018), AI has the capacity to enhance instructional quality through various means, including stimulating classroom discussions (Mageira et al., 2022), offering emotional support (Salas-Pilco, 2020), and enabling personalized learning experiences (Li et al., 2025; Pataranutaporn et al., 2021). While AI tools are increasingly available in schools, their mere pres- ence does not ensure effective pedagogical integration (Dimitriadou & Lanitis, 2023; Filiz et al., 2025; Guan et al., 2025). Actually, given that AI encompasses a suite of emerging and rapidly evolving technologies, teachers may face numerous challenges in the implementation of AI-supported teaching (Chounta et al., 2022; Guan et al., 2025). For instance, some teachers may not possess the requisite technological proficiency in AI, hindering their ability to effectively integrate AI into their teaching practices (Celik et al., 2022). As Chounta et al. (2022) found, due to these challenges, the usage of AI may only slightly increase teachers’ instructional effec- tiveness and efficiency in reality. Thus, understanding and addressing teacher-related factors is critical for unlocking the full potential of AI in education (Filiz et al., 2025; Guan et al., 2025).

Recently, some studies have delved into various teacher-related factors within the realm of AI-supported teaching, encompassing aspects such as adoption (Chou et al., 2024; Du et al., 2024; Li, 2025), perception (Chounta et al., 2022; Niu et al., 2022), knowledge (Celik et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2025; Karataş & Ataç, 2024; Ning et al., 2024), self-efficacy (Du et al., 2024), attitudes (Ayanwale et al., [2025)](#funding) and literacy (Du et

Firstly, none of these existing studies has directly examined how these teacher-related factors influence the quality of AI-supported instruction (e.g. Du et al., 2024; Celik et al., 2022; Chou et al., 2024; Karataş & Ataç, 2024; Li, 2025; Ning et al., 2024; Niu et al., 2022). Celik et al. (2022) have drawn attention to the dearth of empirical research on enhancing the quality of AI-supported teaching from the perspective of teachers. This is further emphasized by Yetişensoy (2024), who stresses that more studies should be conducted to elucidate the mechanisms through which teacher-related factors influence the success of AI-supported instruction. Secondly, existing studies often focus on isolated domains of teacher-related factors, such as knowledge or beliefs, without considering their combined or interactive effects (e.g. Du et al., 2024; Ning et al., 2024; Niu et al., 2022). However, the complexity of AI-supported teaching necessitates a more integrated approach that examines how multiple factors interact to influence instructional quality. Understanding these interrelationships is crucial for developing effective strategies to enhance AI-supported teaching. Thirdly, as noted by Castro et al. (2025), most participants in existing studies are teachers from urban schools (e.g. Ayanwale et al., [2025;](#funding) Chen et al., 2025; Du et al., 2024; Kasmiri & Komalawati, 2024; Li, 2025), while diverse educational con- texts, particularly under-resourced settings such as rural areas, are often overlooked (Castro et al., 2025). This limits the generalizability of findings and leaves critical gaps in the understanding of how teacher-related variables function across varied educational contexts. To address this, researchers should include partici- pants from a broader range of contexts, such as rural, urban, and suburban schools, to enhance the appli- cability and robustness of the findings.

This study examines two antecedents of the quality of AI-supported K–12 teaching. According to Depaepe and König (2018), teachers’ instructional practice is always impacted by two components – professional knowledge and professional beliefs. Our study focuses on one component of professional knowledge, namely AI-technological pedagogical and content knowledge (AI-TPACK), and one component of pro- fessional beliefs, namely self-efficacy in using AI to empower learners (SEEL). On the one hand, AI-TPACK offers a holistic framework that elucidates the intricate interplay between AI, a teacher’s subject matter expertise, and pedagogical strategies, thereby shedding light on the mechanisms by which teachers incor- porate AI into their instructional practice (Karataş & Ataç, 2024; Ning et al., 2024). This framework is pivotal for understanding the cognitive processes and knowledge structures that underpin effective AI integration in teaching. On the other hand, self-efficacy, a critical professional belief, is a robust predictor of the successful implementation of teaching practices and serves as a pivotal metric of a teacher’s capacity to instruct (Jiang et al., 2024a). Teachers with heightened self-efficacy are more likely to adeptly harness AI-driven technol- ogies, thereby amplifying student learning and engagement (Chou et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2024). By bolster- ing self-efficacy in the realm of AI-supported teaching, we can significantly augment teaching efficacy and elevate the caliber of AI-assisted educational initiatives (Yang et al., 2024). In essence, this study aims to uncover how the interplay between AI-TPACK and SEEL influences the quality of AI-supported teaching, pro- viding actionable insights for educational stakeholders and policymakers aiming to optimize AI’s role in enhancing educational outcomes.

Specifically, this study is designed to address the three critical gaps in the existing literature on AI-sup- ported teaching. Firstly, while prior studies explored teacher-related factors such as knowledge, perception, and self-efficacy, none of them empirically examined how these factors directly influence the quality of AI- supported instruction. By investigating the roles of AI-TPACK and SEEL, this study contributes to a deeper understanding of how to enhance the overall quality of AI-supported instruction. Secondly, existing studies often examine teacher-related factors in isolation, overlooking the complex interplay between them. This study adopts an integrated approach by simultaneously considering AI-TPACK and SEEL, thereby exploring how these factors interact to shape teachers’ AI-supported instruction. This holistic per- spective is essential for developing comprehensive frameworks that support effective AI integration in class- rooms. Thirdly, the majority of prior research has focused on urban educational contexts, leaving under- resourced and rural settings underexplored. This study intentionally includes participants from diverse edu- cational contexts, including rural regions, to ensure broader generalizability of the findings.

Our study holds significant practical importance in the following aspects. Firstly, by scrutinizing teachers’ AI-TPACK and SEEL, this study contributes to understanding how prepared teachers are to embrace AI-sup- ported teaching, which is essential for the future-readiness of the education system. For example, for policy- makers, our findings highlight the need to embed AI-TPACK into national teaching standards and teacher 

INTERACTIVE LEARNING ENVIRONMENTS 3

certification frameworks. Secondly, with the increasing integration of AI into instructional practices, there is a notable shift in the adaptability of teaching methods (Shah, 2023). This study aims to equip educators with actionable insights to elevate the caliber of AI-supported teaching. For instance, this study offers guidance on how teachers can augment their AI-TPACK and further cultivate adaptive teaching strategies that harness AI to optimize classroom management, foster a supportive learning environment, and stimulate cognitive engagement. Thirdly, this study yields implications for the development of professional development pro- grams. It helps address the pressing challenge of, rapidly equipping teachers, especially those in underde- veloped regions, to effectively implement AI-supported teaching strategies. For instance, according to our findings, teacher training institutions might consider redesigning curricula to emphasize both technical fluency and psychological readiness. Teachers could engage in scaffolded simulations that require them to integrate AI tools into subject-specific units. These sessions can be coupled with self-efficacy building strategies such as guided reflection, peer feedback, and successful trial teaching with AI tools in controlled settings. By prioritizing the development of AI-TPACK and SEEL in teacher education, educational outcomes can be enhanced by ensuring that teachers are equipped to leverage AI effectively in K-12 classrooms.

# 2. Literature review and hypotheses

Teachers’ professional competence is a multifaceted construct that encompasses both cognitive elements, such as professional knowledge, and affective elements, including professional beliefs (Depaepe & König, 2018). These intertwined components are widely acknowledged to exert a significant influence on instruc- tional practice (e.g. Blömeke & Delaney, 2012; Charalambous, 2015; Depaepe & König, 2018; Yang et al., 2020). Notably, Depaepe and König (2018) claimed that teachers’ self-efficacy is one of the most powerful belief-related antecedents of instructional quality. They further validated a theoretical model postulating that teachers’ instructional practice was significantly predicted by their self-efficacy and general pedagogical knowledge (Depaepe & König, 2018). In addition, Depaepe and König (2018) assumed that when exerting effects on instructional practice, teachers’ professional knowledge and professional beliefs may also be cor- related. However, they failed to confirm this assumption (Depaepe & König, 2018). Although the antecedents of instructional quality are widely discussed in the context of traditional classroom teaching, they have rarely been explored in the context of AI-supported teaching, especially from the perspective of teachers (Celik et al., 2022). We based our theoretical framework on Depaepe and König’s (2018) work and focused on two factors: AI-TPACK and SEEL.

## _2.1. Instructional quality of AI-supported teaching_

Instructional quality is defined as “the degree to which instruction is effective, efficient, and engaging” (Mu et al., 2022, p. 2). Specifically, as [Figure 1](#22-ai-technological-pedagogical-and-content-knowledge-ai-tpack) shows, high-quality instruction can be divided into three dimensions: effective classroom management, supportive climate and cognitive activation (Dorfner et al., 2018; Klieme et al., 2009; Künsting et al., 2016; Schlesinger & Jentsch, 2016). The importance of instructional quality has been widely recognized, as there is compelling evidence for its effects on students’ learning outcomes (Stipek & Chiatovich, 2017). Despite efforts to improve instructional quality in many areas over the past decades, instructional quality still varies considerably within and between schools (Donaldson et al., 2017).

Chen et al. (2020) highlighted the potential of AI to enhance the overall quality of teaching, suggesting that it can support the three dimensions of instructional practice. Firstly, as for classroom management, Alam ([2022)](#funding) pointed out that AI could increase teachers’ monitoring capabilities and thus enhance classroom efficiency. This aligns with Geng et al.’s (2023) findings, which emphasized AI’s role in tracking student beha- viors and offering actionable suggestions to improve classroom dynamics. Furthermore, Timms (2016) observed that AI’s ability to model and predict classroom activities could provide valuable insights, enabling instructors to optimize classroom interactions. These studies collectively demonstrated AI’s capacity to streamline management processes, creating an environment that is more conducive for teaching and learn- ing (Alam, [2022;](#funding) Geng et al., 2023; Timms, 2016).

Secondly, AI also contributes to creating a supportive classroom climate. Seo et al. (2021) illustrated how AI could enable large-scale, personalized interactions between learners and instructors, enhancing both the quantity and quality of communication. This is echoed by Zhang and Chen (2021), who proposed that AI 

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Figure 1.** The three dimensions of high-quality instruction.

could help instructors provide more targeted feedback based on learners’ individual needs and abilities. These studies collectively pointed out that AI may have the potential to foster a more responsive and sup- portive learning environment, ensuring that both learners and instructors benefit from more meaningful engagement (Seo et al., 2021; Zhang & Chen, 2021).

Thirdly, in the domain of cognitive activation, AI’s impact is similarly significant. Samuel et al. (2022) found that AI could reduce cognitive dissonance, which improved cognitive performance, while Liang et al. (2023) provided a broader perspective, showing that AI in language education could stimulate higher-order think- ing skills, such as metacognition, and even influenced learners’ brainwaves. These findings suggests that AI’s potential goes beyond immediate learning tasks, shaping the way learners engage with complex cognitive processes (Liang et al., 2023; Samuel et al., 2022).

Despite the growing body of evidence regarding AI’s potential to enhance various aspects of teaching and learning, the concept of instructional quality in the context of AI-supported teaching has rarely been systematically measured or quantitatively examined (Celik et al., 2022). While numerous studies highlight AI’s promise in improving classroom management (Alam, [2022;](#funding) Geng et al., 2023; Timms, 2016), fostering a supportive classroom climate (Seo et al., 2021; Zhang & Chen, 2021), and enhancing cognitive activation (Liang et al., 2023; Samuel et al., 2022), there remains a significant gap in understanding how these improve- ments translate into measurable gains in instructional quality. To the best of our knowledge, very few studies have set out to assess the instructional quality in the context of AI-supported teaching. Moreover, very few studies have explored the specific actions that teachers can take – or should take – to effectively leverage AI in ways that enhance instructional quality. Teachers are often left to navigate the complexities of AI tools without clear guidance on how to maximize their effectiveness in promoting high-quality instruction. This gap is particularly concerning given the rapidly evolving nature of AI technologies and the increasing pressure on teachers to adapt to these changes.

## _2.2. AI-technological pedagogical and content knowledge (AI-TPACK)_

Sufficient technological knowledge is a prerequisite for using AI technology to support effective teaching (Celik, 2023; Edwards et al., 2018). Based on Shulman’s (1986, 1977) work, Mishra and Koehler (2006) pro- posed the notion of technological pedagogical content knowledge (TPCK) to exhibit the teacher knowledge required for successful technology-supported teaching. Later, Thompson and Mishra (2007) renamed this notion as technological pedagogical and content knowledge (TPACK). For technology-supported teaching specifically, Mishra and Koehler (2008) emphasized the importance of three core components: content, pedagogy and technology. TPACK is defined as a framework that “comprises knowledge of content, 

INTERACTIVE LEARNING ENVIRONMENTS 5

pedagogy, and technology, as well as understanding the complex interaction between these knowledge components” (Mishra & Koehler, 2008, p. 4).

There are two main views on the conceptualization of TPACK (Schmid et al., 2020). On the one hand, taking an integrative stance, some studies consider that TPACK arises from the integration of the knowledge components of content, pedagogy, and technology (e.g. An et al., [2023)](#funding). On the other hand, taking a trans- formative stance, some studies consider TPACK to be one distinct kind of knowledge “which transforms beyond the components at its base” (Schmid et al., 2020, p. 2). Our study adopts the transformative perspec- tive, where TPACK can be assessed separately from those components at its base.

When conceptualizing the notion of TPACK, some specific technologies can be incorporated (Yeh et al., 2021). For example, Lee and Tsai (2010) proposed the notion of Technological Pedagogical Content Knowl- edge-Web (TPCK-W) to describe the knowledge that enables teachers to integrate World Wide Web technol- ogies into their teaching. Recently, the notion of AI-technological pedagogical and content knowledge (AI- TPACK) has been proposed to describe the knowledge base teachers need to integrate AI into teaching (An et al., [2023;](#funding) Park et al., 2023). Figure 2 shows the AI-TPACK framework.

Previous studies have suggested that teachers’ professional knowledge can significantly affect their instructional quality (e.g. Blömeke & Delaney, 2012; Charalambous, 2015; Depaepe & König, 2018; Yang et al., 2020). As for TPACK, although there is a consensus that TPACK, as essential teacher professional knowl- edge, plays a central role in technology-supported teaching (Wang, 2022), the previous findings on the direct impact of TPACK on instructional quality were contradictory. On the one hand, von Kotzebue (2022) found that teachers’ self-reported TPACK could not predict their quality of technology-supported lessons directly. Yao and Lin (2023) also found that TPACK was not a predictor of teaching quality. On the other hand, Ohle- 

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Figure 2.** The AI-TPACK framework.

Peters and Shahat (2023) found that the impact of TPACK on instructional quality was significant. Lu et al. (2023) also found that teachers’ TPACK could significantly predict the quality of their technology integration. As von Kotzebue (2022) pointed out, the inconsistent findings may be caused by the different measurement methods. Furthermore, these inconsistencies may also arise from other underlying factors, such as differ- ences in participant demographics across studies, the diversity of educational settings, and the wide range of technologies and pedagogical strategies employed.

Particularly, prior research has highlighted that the specific features of educational technologies can sig- nificantly influence teaching effectiveness and student learning outcomes (e.g. Cheung & Slavin, 2012; Jiang et al., 2025). Importantly, different types of technology (e.g. learning management systems, virtual reality, or AI-based tools) do not impact instruction in uniform ways. However, the traditional TPACK framework treats technology as a broad, undifferentiated category, without distinguishing among the diverse and rapidly evolving tools available to educators. Nowadays, given the sheer volume and variety of technologies, it is unrealistic to expect teachers to master them all without more focused guidance. This conceptual vagueness may partly explain the inconsistent findings regarding TPACK’s influence on instructional quality. As Schmid et al. (2024) and Willermark (2018) argues, specifying the type of technology under consideration is essential when assessing or applying TPACK, especially if the goal is to generate reliable insights into how teachers use technology to support learning.

In response to the limitations of general TPACK in accounting for specific technologies, this study focuses on AI-TPACK within the context of AI-supported teaching. To date, the impact of AI-TPACK on the quality of AI-supported teaching has rarely been examined. However, some emerging studies suggested that the knowledge components within AI-TPACK could influence the three key dimensions of AI-supported teaching quality individually. For instance, Hava and Babayiğit (2024) have asserted that AI-Technological Pedagogical Knowledge (AI-TPK) encompasses the knowledge needed to utilize AI for effective instructional strategies, including student monitoring and providing constructive feedback. Consequently, teachers with robust AI-TPK are more inclined to adeptly manage classrooms and foster a supportive learning climate through AI applications. Bautista et al. (2024) further suggested that teachers with advanced AI-TPK could leverage AI to stimulate critical thinking by employing strategic teaching methods. Additionally, Ning et al. (2024) demonstrated that teachers with a strong grasp of AI-Technological Content Knowledge (AI-TCK) were more likely to utilize AI to deepen students’ cognitive understanding of subject matter and enhance stu- dents’ cognitive development. Taken together, these emerging studies indicate that AI-TPACK may play a critical role in shaping the quality of AI-supported teaching, particularly across domains such as effective classroom management, supportive climate and cognitive activation. Hence, based on this emerging evi- dence, we assumed that K–12 teachers’ AI-TPACK will significantly affect the quality of their AI-supported teaching. The following hypotheses are proposed:

**H1(a).** K–12 teachers with higher levels of AI-TPACK are more likely to implement effective classroom management with the use of AI.

**H1(b).** K–12 teachers with higher levels of AI-TPACK are more likely to facilitate a supportive climate with the use of AI.

**H1(c).** K–12 teachers with higher levels of AI-TPACK are more likely to enhance cognitive activation in the classroom with the use of AI.

## _2.3. Self-efficacy in using AI to empower learners (SEEL)_

The ultimate goal of using AI in education is to empower learners and augment learners’ intelligence (Ouyang & Jiao, 2021). Specifically, the term _using AI to empower learners_ means that teachers make full use of the interpretable and personalized support provided by AI to implement learner-centered learning, where all learners are able to discover the most effective and appropriate way of developing their knowl- edge, goals and actions (Carvalho et al., 2022; Ouyang & Jiao, 2021). Based on the European framework for the digital competence of educators (Redecker & Punie, 2017) and Runge et al.’s (2023) recommendation, our study conceptualizes _using AI to empower learners_ in two subdimensions: _using AI to actively engage lear-_ _ners_ and _using AI to promote differentiation_. Using AI to actively engage learners means that teachers use AI “to foster learners’ active and creative engagement with a subject matter” (Redecker & Punie, 2017, p. 22). For instance, learners can engage in a joint brainstorming with the use of ChatGPT in the contexts of project- 

INTERACTIVE LEARNING ENVIRONMENTS 7

based learning (Septiani et al., 2023). Using AI to promote differentiation means that teachers use AI “to address learners’ diverse learning needs, by allowing learners to advance at different levels and speeds, and to follow individual learning pathways and objectives” (Redecker & Punie, 2017, p. 22). For instance, in the contexts of task-based learning, AI can provide learners with the most suitable tasks based on learners’ learning pathways and task models (Septiani et al., 2023).

Self-efficacy reflects “people’s beliefs about their capabilities” to perform the designated behavior or tasks (Bandura, 1997, p. 71). In other words, self-efficacy in using AI to empower learners describes teachers’ beliefs about their capability to use AI to empower learners_._ Our study also conceptualizes _self-efficacy in using AI to empower learners_ in two subdimensions: _self-efficacy in using AI to actively engage learners_ and _self-efficacy in using AI to promote differentiation_. As the ultimate goal of using AI in education is to empower learners (Ouyang & Jiao, 2021), enhancing teachers’ self-efficacy in using AI to empower learners can also be regarded as one of the ultimate goals of teacher education in the age of AI.

The impact of teachers’ self-efficacy on instructional quality has been widely confirmed (e.g. Burić & Kim, 2020; Holzberger et al., 2013; Thommen et al., 2022). As Sitzmann and Yeo (2013) pointed out, self-efficacy has direct and positive effects on individuals’ performance. As such, if teachers have high levels of self- efficacy, they will consider themselves competent in instruction, which in turn contributes to high-quality instruction (Thommen et al., 2022). However, this impact has barely been examined in the contexts of AI-sup- ported teaching. We assume that if teachers have high levels of SEEL, then they are more likely to realize the ultimate goal of integrating AI in education (empower learners), and thus the quality of their AI-supported teaching is more likely to be high. The hypothesis is as follows: 

**H2(a).** K–12 teachers with higher levels of self-efficacy in using AI to actively engage learners are more likely to implement effective classroom management with the use of AI.

**H2(b).** K–12 teachers with higher levels of self-efficacy in using AI to actively engage learners are more likely to facilitate a supportive climate with the use of AI.

**H2(c).** K–12 teachers with higher levels of self-efficacy in using AI to actively engage learners are more likely to enhance cognitive activation in the classroom with the use of AI.

**H2(d).** K–12 teachers with higher levels of self-efficacy in using AI to promote differentiation are more likely to implement effective classroom management with the use of AI.

**H2(e).** K–12 teachers with higher levels of self-efficacy in using AI to promote differentiation are more likely to facilitate a supportive climate with the use of AI.

**H2(f).** K–12 teachers with higher levels of self-efficacy in using AI to promote differentiation are more likely to enhance cognitive activation in the classroom with the use of AI.

Bandura (1977) claimed that mastery experiences, namely experiences where individuals perform a given behavior and achieve specified goals, could be regarded as a source of self-efficacy. Raudenbush et al. (1992) further propose that self-efficacy is a mediator between knowledge and action. As Raudenbush et al. (1992) point out, if teachers possess sufficient knowledge required in high-quality instruction, they are likely to implement high-quality instruction, and those experiences of high-quality instruction will further enhance their self-efficacy. Their statement has also been empirically justified in recent studies (e.g. Bjerke & Solomon, 2020).

TPACK is frequently used to represent the knowledge required for successful technology-supported teaching (Mishra & Koehler, 2006). In the contexts of technology-supported teaching, prior studies have revealed that TPACK could significantly affect teachers’ self-efficacy beliefs (Abbitt, [2011;](#funding) Jin & Harp, 2020). For instance, Jin and Harp (2020) pointed out that TPACK could help teachers generate strong self- efficacy beliefs in teaching with technology integration. Furthermore, it is reasonable to assume that if tea- chers have high levels of AI-TPACK, namely knowledge required for integrating AI into teaching, they may have successful experiences of using AI to empower learners in the classroom, and their self-efficacy in using AI to empower learners will be strong. However, this assumption has never been validated in the context of AI-supported teaching. Our hypotheses are as follows: 

**H3(a).** K–12 teachers with higher levels of AI-TPACK will have higher levels of self-efficacy in using AI to actively engage learners.

Note. SEPD refers to self-efficacy in using AI to promote differentiation, SEAEL refers to self-efficacy in using AI to actively engage learners, AICM refers to AI-enhanced classroom management, AISC refers to AI-enhanced supportive climate, and AICA refers to AI-enhanced cognitive activation. SEPD and SEAEL are the two subdimensions of self-efficacy in using AI to empower learners. AICM, AISC and AICA are the three subdimensions of instructional quality of AI-supported teaching.

**H3(b).** K–12 teachers with higher levels of AI-TPACK will have higher levels of self-efficacy in using AI to promote differentiation.

[Figure 3](#3-method) illustrates the hypotheses proposed based on the aforementioned literature. In light of Depaepe and König (2018), we assume that K–12 teachers’ self-reported quality of AI-supported teaching will be impacted by two factors: AI-TPACK and SEEL. Notably, SEEL encompasses two subdimensions of SEEL (i.e. SEPD and SEAEL). AI-TPACK will influence the quality of AI-supported teaching not only directly but also indirectly via the two subdimensions of SEEL.

# 3. Method

## _3.1. Procedure and participants_

To enhance the representativeness of our sample, this study selected three K–12 schools from urban, sub- urban and rural areas at random. In each area (i.e. urban, suburban, and rural), one elementary school, one junior high school and one senior high school were selected. As such, a total of nine K–12 schools were selected. Following a proportionate stratified random sampling procedure, we collected data from K–12 tea- chers in different areas. Specifically, we randomly selected 500 K–12 teachers in each area, respectively, and invited them to participate in our research through emails sent by school administrators. If teachers who received the email agreed to participate in our research, we asked them to fill in the online questionnaire we had provided. We confirmed that they had experience implementing AI-supported teaching for at least one month before they filled in the online questionnaire. We did not send the online questionnaire link to teachers who did not have or had little experience integrating AI in teaching. According to Zhang and Aslan (2021), the most widely used types of AI in teaching include: chatbots, expert systems, intelligent tutors, machine learning, personalized learning systems, visualizations, and virtual learning environments. All participants had more than one month of experience of using at least one kind of the aforementioned AI in their classrooms. Ethical approval was obtained from the first author’s university before we collected data.

We received 999 responses, but 68 responses were incomplete and thus were removed from the final data set. Hence, our sample included a total of 931 teachers. The effective rate was 93.19%. [Table 1](#32-instruments) shows the participants’ demographic information.

## _3.2. Instruments_

This study adapted three instruments, all of which were in the form of 7-point Likert scales. Specifically, the first instrument, aiming to measure teachers’ self-reported instructional quality in the context of AI-sup- ported teaching, was adapted and modified based on Rubach and Lazarides’s (2021) and Runge et al.’s (2023) work. In accordance with these scholars, our first instrument included three subdimensions, namely AI-enhanced cognitive activation, AI-enhanced supportive climate, and AI-enhanced classroom man- agement. The second instrument, aiming to measure AI-TPACK, was adapted and modified based on Celik’s (2023) work. The third instrument, aiming to measure SEEL, was adapted and modified based on Runge et al.’s (2023) work. In accordance with Runge et al. (2023), our third instrument included two subdimensions, namely self-efficacy in using AI to actively engage learners and self-efficacy in using AI to promote differentiation.

Our process for adapting the instruments involved six key steps (Jiang et al., 2023). Initially, we created a preliminary English version of the instrument, drawing on relevant literature for its components (see [Table 2)](#32-instruments). Next, we adhered to the guidelines set forth by Guillemin et al. (1993) and Klarare et al. (2021) to translate the

instrument into Chinese, ensuring both forward and back-translations were accurately executed. Following that, we sought feedback from language and educational specialists, refining the instrument based on their recommendations. In the fourth phase, to validate the three instruments, we conducted a pilot test on 312 teachers. These teachers were asked to provide personal feedback on the instruments upon completion. Consequently, we made adjustments by revising or eliminating certain items based on the teachers’ feed- back to make our expressions in the instruments more concise. Finally, we conducted an Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA) to assess the initial reliability and validity of the instrument. The pilot instrument con- sisted of 23 translated items grouped into six factors. However, the EFA results from the rotated component matrix revealed nine components. Among them, Components 7 to 9 were each measured by a single item with factor loadings below the acceptable threshold of 0.45, and each had eigenvalues less than 1. Based on these statistical criteria, three items (AITPK1, SEPD1, and SEAEL2) were excluded from further analysis due to insufficient validity.

After removing these items, three shortened and modified instruments were used in the formal data collection. We also tested the reliability and validity of the three modified instruments using the formal data set and reported them in the Results section. Detailed information about the three instruments is shown in [Table 3.](#33-data-analysis)

## _3.3. Data analysis_

This study adopted a structural equation modeling approach to analyze the data (Thakkar, 2020). Using AMOS version 21, we performed the analysis in two steps. Firstly, we tested the measurement model and reported the reliability and validity of the three instruments. The stability of the model was also cross-vali- dated with two sub-datasets, namely STEM teachers and non-STEM teachers. Secondly, we tested the hypotheses and calculated the effects of AI-TPACK and SEEL on the quality of teachers’ AI-supported teach- ing. Notably, six variables (i.e. gender, age, area, stage, educational background, and subject) were controlled in the data analysis.

# 4. Results

Using AMOS version 21, we drew the measurement model and interrelated the six latent variables in our conceptual model to compute average variance extracted (AVE\> .50), composite reliability (CR \> .70) and covariances (\<√AVE) to provide evidence for the convergent validity (Hair et al., 2010), as reported in Table 4. The factor loadings for all indicators are statistically significant, as noted by Hair et al. (2010). For discriminant validity (Fornell & Larcker, 1981), we confirmed that the square roots of the AVEs were higher than the interrelationships among factors. We judged our confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) findings for the modified model’s fit indices with the recommended values (Byrne, 2010, p. 80), as follows: “chi-square (_χ_2)/degree of freedom (\< 5), root mean square error of approximation (RMSEA \< .1), Tucker–Lewis Index (TLI \> .90) and comparative fit index (CFI \> .90)”. Then, we found good model fit statistics, _χ_2 = 737.454; df = 155; _p_ = .000; RMSEA = .064; CFI = .987; and TLI = .984.

Later, we drew the path diagram (see Figure 4) to test our 11 proposed hypotheses, of which 8 were valid, as confirmed by the path coefficients (_β_), critical ratios (CR) and _p_ values of the structural model. The model had good fit statistics, _χ_2 = 547.628; df = 159; _p_ = .000; RMSEA = .067; CFI = .969; and TLI = .963. The findings indicated that K–12 teachers with higher levels of AI-TPACK were more likely to implement effective

# 5. Discussion

## _5.1. Theoretical contributions_

There is a pressing need for more research to explore how to improve the quality of AI-supported teaching from the perspective of teachers (Celik et al., 2022; Yetişensoy, 2024). This study responded to the research need and has several significant theoretical contributions.

First of all, one of our most significant theoretical contributions is the confirmation of the direct impact of AI-TPACK on the quality of AI-supported teaching. While previous research underscored the substan- tial influence of teacher knowledge on instructional quality (e.g. Blömeke & Delaney, 2012; Charalam- bous, 2015; Depaepe & König, 2018; Yang et al., 2020), a consensus on the significance of this influence, particularly regarding TPACK’s role in instructional quality, has been elusive. Specifically, Lu et al. (2023) and Ohle-Peters and Shahat (2023) detected a notable impact of TPACK on instructional quality, yet von Kotzebue (2022) found that teachers’ self-reported TPACK did not directly predict the quality of their technology-supported lessons. Similarly, Yao and Lin (2023) concluded that TPACK was not a reliable predictor of teaching quality. In the realm of AI-supported teaching, the influence of AI- TPACK on instructional quality has remained unexplored until now. Our research stands at the forefront, delivering groundbreaking empirical evidence that underscores the significant effects of AI-TPACK on the instructional quality of AI-supported teaching. This result is consistent with the findings of Lu et al. (2023) and Ohle-Peters and Shahat (2023), yet it diverges from the outcomes reported by von Kotzebue (2022) and Yao and Lin (2023).

Several underlying factors might explain these inconsistencies. On the one hand, the TPACK framework is inherently dynamic and in a state of perpetual evolution (Shambare & Simuja, 2024). The rapid pace of tech- nological advancement ensures that the technological knowledge components within TPACK are subject to ongoing transformation (Ning et al., 2024), which can result in divergent findings across various studies. In essence, the impact of different technologies on teaching quality can be markedly different (Jiang et al., 2025). When compared to traditional information and communication technologies, AI stands out for its immense potential to enhance teaching quality. It does so by offering personalized and adaptive learning experiences to students, deepening teachers’ comprehension of their students’ learning trajectories, and enabling ubiquitous access to machine-supported inquiries and prompt feedback (Chiu et al., 2023). The AI-TPACK model builds upon the foundational elements of the traditional TPACK framework but goes further by integrating knowledge components specific to AI technologies. This integration could lead to the development of more effective instructional practices that leverage the unique capabilities of AI. On the other hand, the context-dependent nature of TPACK may also contribute to these inconsistencies (Sham- bare & Simuja, 2024). Indeed, while the importance of TPACK is well recognized, recent studies have empha- sized that the successful integration of technology into teaching is not only about possessing TPACK but also significantly depends on whether teachers can effectively apply TPACK within their unique instructional con- texts (Shambare & Simuja, 2024; Tschönhens et al., 2024). The instructional context, teachers’ experience and students’ demographics vary widely across different countries and cultures. These differences could influence how TPACK was applied and its subsequent impact on the instructional quality (Sofwan et al., 2023; Tschönhens et al., 2024). In addition, as von Kotzebue (2022) pointed out, the different methods in measuring TPACK and instructional quality may also cause inconsistent findings.

The varying effects of TPACK on instructional quality indeed highlight the intricate nature of integrating educational technology into the classroom. This complexity underscores the necessity for sustained research into the development and measurement of the TPACK framework, particularly focusing on how teachers apply TPACK within their distinct instructional settings. Such research is crucial for understanding the nuances of technology integration and for refining the TPACK framework to better suit the evolving needs of educators. It is worth noting that AI-TPACK is a novel construct, and very few studies have focused on it (Ning et al., 2024). This study emphasizes the importance of AI-TPACK and calls for more research on its theoretical construct and how it is practically applied in different instructional contexts.

INTERACTIVE LEARNING ENVIRONMENTS 13

Secondly, our research delves into the intricate interplay between the subdimensions of teachers’ self- efficacy and their instructional quality within the realm of AI-supported teaching. This exploration uncovers how different aspects of teachers’ self-efficacy can significantly impact the effectiveness of their instruction when AI is integrated into the classroom. Although the impact of teachers’ self-efficacy on instructional quality has been widely confirmed (e.g. Burić & Kim, 2020; Holzberger et al., 2013; Thommen et al., 2022), prior studies have seldom examined the impact of self-efficacy in different subdimensions on instructional quality. Our findings contributed to the literature by revealing that teachers’ self-efficacy in using AI to actively engage learners can significantly impact the quality of AI-supported teaching, while teachers’ self-efficacy in using AI to promote differentiation will likely not have a significant impact. Particularly, the two subdimensions of SEEL were adapted from Runge et al. (2023). Their study was set in the context of tech- nology-enhanced teaching and found that teachers’ digital competence-related beliefs regarding actively engaging learners did not significantly affect instructional quality, and their digital competence-related beliefs regarding differentiation could only significantly affect two subdimensions of instructional quality. In this sense, our findings were totally different from theirs.

There are some potential reasons for the different results. On the one hand, Runge et al.’s (2023) research was conducted within the broader context of technology-enhanced teaching, whereas our study focused specifically on AI-supported teaching. This distinction is significant, as the scope of our study is more special- ized. Given the sophisticated role of AI in educational technology, the context of AI-supported teaching may encompass unique characteristics not present in the more general technology-enhanced teaching context. For example, when compared to traditional educational technologies, AI, especially generative AI, has the potential to significantly enhance student engagement in the learning process (Almusaed et al., [2023;](#funding) Chiu et al., 2024). This enhanced engagement is a critical indicator of high-quality teaching (Early et al., 2014). Specifically, engaged students are more likely to concentrate on learning rather than disruptive beha- viors, reducing the need for teachers’ management (Scott et al., 2014). An engaged classroom fosters inclu- sivity, with all students participating and feeling valued, leading to a more supportive and collaborative environment (Duchaine & Fain, 2018). Engaged students are also more likely to be cognitively active, proces- sing information deeply rather than passively receiving it (Floyd et al., 2009). Consequently, teachers with higher levels of self-efficacy in using AI to actively engage learners are more likely to implement effective classroom management, cultivate a supportive climate, and promote cognitive activation through AI. On the other hand, cultural values and educational systems can shape teachers’ self-efficacy and instructional practices in profound ways (Romijn et al., 2020). Since Runge et al.’s (2023) study and ours were conducted in Western and Chinese cultures, respectively, teachers’ self-efficacy, instructional quality, and their interplay may be significantly influenced by these distinct cultural and educational contexts (Romijn et al., 2020; Vieluf et al., 2013). For instance, Chinese culture places a higher value on collectivism (Jiang et al., 2024b). In col- lectivist cultures, there is a strong emphasis on group harmony and avoiding actions that might disrupt the group’s unity (Luo et al., 2013). This cultural emphasis may lead teachers and students to prioritize group goals over individual learning objectives and needs, potentially mitigating the impact of teachers’ self- efficacy in using AI to promote differentiation in their instructional quality. In addition to culture-related moderating variables, other factors, such as students’ acceptance of AI, may also significantly influence the relationship between teachers’ self-efficacy and instructional quality within the context of AI-supported teaching.

Thirdly, our research elucidates the pivotal mediating roles that teachers’ professional beliefs play between their professional knowledge and instructional practice. Depaepe and König (2018) assumed that when informing instructional practice, teachers’ professional knowledge and professional beliefs may be correlated. However, they failed to confirm this assumption (Depaepe & König, 2018). Our study confirmed the mediation effects of AI-TPACK on instructional quality via self-efficacy in using AI to actively engage learners. In other words, when informing instructional practice, AI-TPACK, as one kind of teachers’ professional knowledge, was linked with teachers’ self-efficacy in using AI to actively engage learners, as one kind of teachers’ professional beliefs. This indicated that the successful integration of AI into teaching is not merely about possessing AI-TPACK knowledge; it is also contingent upon teachers’ beliefs to apply this knowledge effectively within the unique contexts of their teaching. In essence, our study provides new insights into the exploration of the relationships among teachers’ professional knowledge, professional beliefs and instructional quality, and thus contributes to the existing literature. Our findings underscore the 

intricate interplay among what teachers know, what they believe, and how they actually teach, and reveal the importance of considering teachers’ beliefs as critical mediating factors. These beliefs significantly influence how professional knowledge is translated into practice, especially in the context of AI-supported teaching.

Lastly, building on Rubach and Lazarides (2021) and Runge et al. (2023), this study proposed that the theoretical construct of the instructional quality of AI-supported teaching included AI-enhanced cognitive activation, AI-enhanced supportive climate, and AI-enhanced classroom management. Our study justified this theoretical construct by confirming that our instrument has satisfactory reliability and validity. This theoretical construct can also provide insights into assessing the instructional quality of AI-supported teach- ing by classroom observations, students’ feedback and other methods. Moreover, it can also guide future research, policy-making, and professional development efforts aimed at optimizing AI’s contribution to the process and outcomes of teaching.

## _5.2. Practical implications_

Given the accelerating integration of AI into K–12 classrooms, improving the quality of AI-supported teach- ing is both urgent and foundational for future-ready education. The findings of this study offer a set of actionable insights for practitioners and policymakers seeking to build capacity for effective AI integration.

Our findings confirm that AI-TPACK is a strong and consistent predictor of the instructional quality of AI- supported teaching. This underscores the need to treat AI-TPACK not as a peripheral skillset but as a core component of teacher education and professional development. Building AI-TPACK requires moving beyond superficial “tool training” to a more disciplined, context-sensitive approach. Teachers must learn not only how AI tools work, but also when and why to use them (Zhang, 2021). Specifically, teachers must master not only the mechanics of AI applications but also the nuanced decisions of when to deploy them, for which learning objectives, and in service of which pedagogical values.

Developing AI-TPACK begins with subject-relevant exploration. Teachers should start by familiarizing themselves with AI tools aligned to their content areas, using resources such as Google’s AI Fundamentals or Coursera’s Generative AI for Educators to build foundational knowledge. Discipline-specific integration makes this learning meaningful. For example, a math teacher might use Wolfram Alpha to demonstrate multi-step solutions and reinforce problem-solving strategies; a history teacher could use ChatGPT to gen- erate historical debate prompts, encouraging critical thinking and empathy; science educators might incor- porate AI-powered simulations to model complex phenomena like climate change; and language teachers can leverage AI writing assistants to support student writing from brainstorming through revision. At the same time, teachers must cultivate a critical mindset – cross-checking AI-generated content for accuracy, rel- evance, and bias. For example, verifying the sources of an AI-generated historical summary or double-check- ing algorithm-generated math solutions for correctness.

The transformative power of AI in education lies not in the tools themselves, but in how intentionally and meaningfully they are embedded within instruction. Effective integration depends on teachers’ ability to align AI tools with curricular goals and use them to enhance student thinking, creativity, and engagement. This process is neither intuitive nor static – it demands ongoing critical reflection about the affordances, limitations, and ethical implications of AI in the classroom. Zhang (2021) argues that cultivating AI-TPACK is not merely a technical endeavor but a reflective one: teachers must critically examine how, when, and why AI intersects with their pedagogical content knowledge. One effective strategy for building this reflec- tive capacity is adopting a practice-based inquiry cycle. Teachers can begin by systematically documenting AI-integrated lessons in a digital journal or blog, noting not just what worked, but also challenges, unex- pected student responses, and ethical questions that arose. Including student prompts, AI outputs, task revi- sions, and short analytical notes can help link classroom observations to broader instructional objectives. Over time, these records become a personal evidence base from which patterns of effective practice emerge. Reflection also gains power when it becomes collaborative. Teachers should be encouraged to share annotated lesson excerpts in professional learning communities or shared repositories, where col- leagues can respond with feedback and suggestions.

School systems and education ministries should implement tiered professional development models that progressively build AI-TPACK. Introductory workshops can cover foundational AI literacy and ethical 

INTERACTIVE LEARNING ENVIRONMENTS 15

awareness; intermediate modules can focus on discipline-specific strategies and case studies; and advanced tracks can offer hands-on design sprints where teachers prototype and test AI-infused lessons. As suggested by Yeh et al. (2021), these programs might also be grounded in professional learning communities that foster sustained peer learning, reflective dialogue, and shared experimentation.

For policymakers, our findings highlight the need to embed AI-TPACK into national teaching standards, teacher certification frameworks, and curriculum guidelines. This could involve revising national teaching standards to include explicit benchmarks for AI-TPACK, such as the ability to select appropriate AI tools aligned with subject content and learning goals. Teacher certification processes should also assess candi- dates’ capacity to design, implement, and evaluate AI-supported instruction, ensuring that future educators enter the workforce equipped to teach in AI-enhanced environments. Additionally, policymakers can fund the development of AI-TPACK-aligned teaching rubrics, sample lesson repositories, and assessment tools to support implementation at the classroom level. Pilot programs that integrate AI-TPACK into teacher train- ing institutes, especially in underserved regions, could serve as scalable models, supported by national or regional investment.

Secondly, our study highlights the important role of SEAEL as a significant predictor of instructional quality. While research has shown that AI can significantly enhance student engagement (Ouyang et al., 2022), many teachers remain unaware of how to leverage this potential. Building SEAEL requires more than theoretical understanding; it depends on teachers gaining first-hand, successful experiences that build confidence in using AI effectively. To facilitate this, professional development programs should incor- porate guided classroom trials where teachers can pilot AI tools in low-stakes settings, supported by coach- ing or peer mentorship. For example, teachers might implement short AI-enhanced activities such as using intelligent tutoring systems for personalized feedback or AI chatbots for reflective journaling. These experi- ences should be paired with structured reflection sessions that review student engagement metrics (e.g. time-on-task, participation rates, or student feedback) collected through the AI tools themselves. When tea- chers observe clear, positive shifts in student motivation, curiosity, or interaction, their belief in the value of AI-supported instruction is likely to grow. This aligns with Bandura’s (1997) theory of mastery experiences as a primary driver of self-efficacy. Furthermore, training programs can deepen this effect by integrating student perspective sessions, where learners share how AI tools have influenced their engagement, learning experience, or motivation. Hearing directly from students can help teachers validate the practical value of AI not just from an instructional standpoint, but from the learner’s point of view.

In addition, policy initiatives can support SEAEL development by recognizing and rewarding teachers who demonstrate innovative and effective AI use. For example, districts could implement micro-credentialing systems where teachers earn badges or certificates for designing and executing successful AI-supported lessons. These recognitions not only validate teacher effort but also build a culture that values experimen- tation and digital leadership.

Lastly, our findings indicate that AI-TPACK also indirectly influences instructional quality by enhancing SEAEL, suggesting that these constructs are mutually reinforcing. This underscores the importance of tea- chers actively applying their AI-TPACK not just to deliver content, but to design learning experiences that fully engage students. For example, teachers can leverage their AI-TPACK to create real-world, interdisciplin- ary tasks where students use AI tools to analyze local community data (e.g. pollution levels or energy con- sumption) and propose actionable solutions. These tasks support both content mastery and authentic problem-solving, which in turn heightens student motivation and engagement. Moreover, AI-TPACK sup- ports collaborative, student-centered learning. As Maor (2017) notes, TPACK can pave “the way for educators to engage students in collaborative learning” (p. 83), and AI can amplify this by enabling shared digital work- spaces where students co-construct knowledge. For instance, AI tools can facilitate group project planning, real-time feedback, and multilingual collaboration through features like automatic translation. These appli- cations move AI use beyond automation and into the realm of inquiry-based, participatory learning. When teachers use AI strategically in these ways, they may build confidence in their ability to engage learners, thus further improving their instructional quality.

In summary, this study extends beyond theoretical contribution to provide concrete, scalable strategies for operationalizing AI-TPACK and SEEL in professional development, classroom practice, and policy initiat- ives. By aligning teacher training, peer support structures, and policy incentives around these two constructs, 

education systems can better equip their teaching workforce to navigate the challenges and realize the full potential of AI in K–12 education.

## _5.3. Limitations and future directions_

This study is not without limitations. First of all, in our study, K–12 teachers’ instructional quality was measured using a self-reported scale. On the one hand, Runge et al. (2023) claimed that, when assessing instructional quality, self-reports could help researchers achieve valid results. On the other hand, Runge et al. (2023) also pointed out that there were hardly any methods to measure instructional quality totally based on objective tests. Hence, based on Runge et al.’s (2023) arguments, we decided to measure instruc- tional quality using self-reports. However, it is unavoidable that some teachers over- or underestimate the quality of their AI-supported teaching. It is recommended that future studies also collect other data sources (e.g. classroom observations, students’ feedback or assessment) to increase the accuracy of the measurement of instructional quality. Secondly, many factors may influence the quality of AI-supported teaching, but it is impossible to examine all of the potential factors in one single study. Our study is guided by Depaepe and König’s (2018) framework and tested the impact of AI-TPACK and SEEL on instruc- tional quality in the context of AI-supported teaching. Future studies can explore more potential factors based on our model. Thirdly, considering the ultimate goal of using AI in education is to empower learners, this study focused on SEEL when talking about teachers’ self-efficacy. However, the goals of using AI in edu- cation are multi-dimensional. Future studies can focus on teachers’ self-efficacy in other dimensions.

Last but not least, this study represents a component of a broader research initiative that is exploring AI- supported teaching practices among Chinese teachers (Du et al., 2024). The current study is grounded in quantitative data analysis, but subsequent phases of this research will integrate qualitative data sources. These will encompass comprehensive teacher interviews and open-ended survey responses, offering insights into the underlying motivations and experiences that inform teachers’ perceptions of self-efficacy and instructional quality in the AI-supported teaching context. This approach will also elucidate the non-sig- nificant impact of teachers’ self-efficacy in using AI to promote differentiation on instructional quality, enrich- ing our understanding of the intricate interplay among teachers’ professional knowledge, beliefs, and instructional quality.

# 6. Conclusion

This study examined two antecedents of K–12 teachers’ self-reported instructional quality in the context of AI-supported teaching, namely AI-TPACK and SEEL. Specifically, SEEL is conceptualized in two subdimen- sions: self-efficacy in using AI to actively engage learners and self-efficacy in using AI to promote differen- tiation. Instructional quality in the context of AI-supported teaching is conceptualized in three subdimensions: AI-enhanced classroom management, AI-enhanced supportive climate, and AI-enhanced cognitive activation. Our findings showed that K–12 teachers’ AI-TPACK and self-efficacy in using AI to actively engage learners significantly impacted the three subdimensions of instructional quality, while the impact of self-efficacy in using AI to promote differentiation was not significant. The mediation effects of AI-TPACK on the three subdimensions of instructional quality via self-efficacy in using AI to actively engage learners were also confirmed. This study filled in a research gap by theoretically revealing two sig- nificant predictors of the instructional quality of AI-supported teaching and has important practical impli- cations on how to improve the quality of AI-supported teaching.

***Haozhe Jiang*** is a ZJU100 Young Professor at the College of Education of Zhejiang University. His research interests include educational technology, curriculum and instruction, and teacher education. He has published in the International Journal of STEM Education, Journal of Research in Science Teaching, International Journal of Educational Research, and some other international journals.

***A.Y.M. Atiquil Islam*** is an associate professor at the Department of Education Information Technology of East China Normal University. He is also an Honorary Chair Professor at the School of Teacher Education, Jiangsu University. He has had almost 21 years of experience in academia, industry and business. Leading from the front, he has been conduct- ing workshops on the application of Structural Equation Modeling and Rasch Model since 2010. He has published nearly 90 papers in first-class international journals and conferences. Dr. Islam is an Executive Editor of the International Journal of Smart Technology and Learning, Editor of Cogent Education (ESCI & Scopus), and Article Editor of SAGE Open (SSCI). His research interests are in the arena of Assessment of Educational Technology, Quantitative Modeling, Artificial Intelli- gence, ICT in Higher Education, Technology, People & Society, Technical and Vocational Education and Training, Edu- cational Research, Information Systems, Human Computer Interaction, Information Science, Digital Library Sciences, e- learning, New Social Media Analysis and Virtual Reality.

***Michael Agyemang Adarkwah*** is a Research Associate at the Institute of Education and Culture at Friedrich-Schiller-Uni- versität Jena (University of Jena). His research interests are; artificial intelligence (AI) in adult learning, digitalization, com- puters and education, special education, teaching and learning, motivation, assessment, linguistics, and healthcare research. Michael is an international expert peer reviewer. He has reviewed for multiple educational technology journals. He is part of the editorial board of the Journal of Educational Studies and Multidisciplinary Approaches (JESMA), the Inter- national Journal of Modern Education Studies (IJONMES), and Social Education Research (SER). He is an Associate Editor for SN Social Sciences.
